sectionOrArticle: Article I: Of Faith in the Holy Trinity
citation: Wesleyan Articles of Religion, Art. I (1784)
topic: The Holy Trinity: One Living and True God
coreDoctrine: There is but one living and true God, everlasting, without body or parts, of infinite power, wisdom, and goodness; the maker and preserver of all things, visible and invisible. And in unity of this Godhead there are three persons, of one substance, power, and eternity—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost.
fullExcerpt: There is but one living and true God, everlasting, without body or parts, of infinite power, wisdom, and goodness; the maker and preserver of all things, visible and invisible. And in unity of this Godhead there are three persons, of one substance, power, and eternity—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost.

sectionOrArticle: Article II: Of the Word, or Son of God, Who Was Made Very Man
citation: Wesleyan Articles of Religion, Art. II (1784)
topic: The Incarnation, Two Natures, Virgin Birth & Universal Atonement
coreDoctrine: The Son, who is the Word of the Father, the very and eternal God, of one substance with the Father, took man’s nature in the womb of the blessed Virgin, of her substance: so that two whole and perfect natures, that is to say, the Godhead and Manhood, were joined together in one person, never to be divided, whereof is one Christ, very God and very man, who truly suffered, was crucified, dead, and buried, to reconcile His Father to us, and to be a sacrifice, not only for original guilt, but also for actual sins of men.
fullExcerpt: The Son, who is the Word of the Father, the very and eternal God, of one substance with the Father, took man’s nature in the womb of the blessed Virgin, of her substance: so that two whole and perfect natures, that is to say, the Godhead and Manhood, were joined together in one person, never to be divided, whereof is one Christ, very God and very man, who truly suffered, was crucified, dead, and buried, to reconcile His Father to us, and to be a sacrifice, not only for original guilt, but also for actual sins of men.

sectionOrArticle: Articles III & IV: Resurrection of Christ & The Holy Ghost
citation: Wesleyan Articles of Religion, Art. III & IV (1784)
topic: Resurrection, Ascension and the Holy Ghost
coreDoctrine: Christ did truly rise again from the dead, and took again His body, with all things appertaining to the perfection of man’s nature, wherewith He ascended into heaven, and there sitteth until He return to judge all men at the last day (Art. III). The Holy Ghost, proceeding from the Father and the Son, is of one substance, majesty, and glory with the Father and the Son, very and eternal God (Art. IV).
fullExcerpt: Christ did truly rise again from the dead, and took again His body, with all things appertaining to the perfection of man’s nature, wherewith He ascended into heaven, and there sitteth until He return to judge all men at the last day (Art. III). The Holy Ghost, proceeding from the Father and the Son, is of one substance, majesty, and glory with the Father and the Son, very and eternal God (Art. IV).

sectionOrArticle: Articles V & VI: Sufficiency of Holy Scriptures & The Old Testament
citation: Wesleyan Articles of Religion, Art. V & VI (1784)
topic: Sufficiency of Scripture for Salvation & The Moral Law
coreDoctrine: The Holy Scriptures contain all things necessary to salvation; so that whatever is not read therein, nor may be proved thereby, is not to be required of any man that it should be believed as an article of faith. The Old Testament is not contrary to the New: for both in the Old and New Testament everlasting life is offered to mankind by Christ; no Christian man whatsoever is free from obedience to the Moral Commandments.
fullExcerpt: The Holy Scriptures contain all things necessary to salvation; so that whatever is not read therein, nor may be proved thereby, is not to be required of any man that it should be believed as an article of faith, or be thought requisite or necessary to salvation. In the name of the Holy Scripture, we do understand those canonical books of the Old and New Testament of whose authority was never any doubt in the Church (Art. V). The Old Testament is not contrary to the New; for both in the Old and New Testament everlasting life is offered to mankind by Christ, who is the only Mediator between God and man, being both God and man... Although the law given from God by Moses as touching ceremonies and rites doth not bind Christians, yet no Christian man whatsoever is free from the obedience of the commandments which are called moral (Art. VI).

sectionOrArticle: Articles VII & VIII: Of Original Sin & Free Will (Prevenient Grace)
citation: Wesleyan Articles of Religion, Art. VII & VIII (1784)
topic: Original Sin, Fallen Nature & Prevenient Grace
coreDoctrine: Original sin is the corruption of the nature of every man naturally engendered of the offspring of Adam, whereby man is very far gone from original righteousness, and of his own nature inclined to evil continually (Art. VII). The condition of man after the fall is such that he cannot turn and prepare himself by his own natural strength to faith and calling upon God, without the grace of God by Christ preventing (enabling) us, that we may have a good will, and working with us when we have that good will (Art. VIII).
fullExcerpt: Original sin standeth not in the following of Adam (as the Pelagians do vainly talk), but it is the corruption of the nature of every man, that naturally is engendered of the offspring of Adam, whereby man is very far gone from original righteousness, and of his own nature inclined to evil, and that continually (Art. VII). The condition of man after the fall of Adam is such that he cannot turn and prepare himself, by his own natural strength and works, to faith, and calling upon God; wherefore we have no power to do good works, pleasant and acceptable to God, without the grace of God by Christ preventing us, that we may have a good will, and working with us, when we have that good will (Art. VIII).

sectionOrArticle: Articles IX, X & XI: Justification, Good Works & Works of Supererogation
citation: Wesleyan Articles of Religion, Art. IX–XI (1784)
topic: Justification by Faith, Fruits of Faith, and Supererogation Rejected
coreDoctrine: We are accounted righteous before God only for the merit of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, by faith, and not for our own works or deservings: wherefore, that we are justified by faith only is a most wholesome doctrine, and very full of comfort (Art. IX). Good works are the necessary fruits of faith, following after justification (Art. X). Works of supererogation cannot be taught without arrogancy and impiety (Art. XI).
fullExcerpt: We are accounted righteous before God, only for the merit of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, by faith, and not for our own works or deservings: wherefore, that we are justified by faith only is a most wholesome doctrine, and very full of comfort (Art. IX). Although good works, which are the fruits of faith, and follow after justification, cannot put away our sins, and endure the severity of God’s judgment; yet are they pleasing and acceptable to God in Christ, and spring out of a true and lively faith, insomuch that by them a lively faith may be as evidently known as a tree discerned by its fruit (Art. X). Voluntary works, besides, over and above God’s commandments, which are called works of supererogation, cannot be taught without arrogancy and impiety (Art. XI).

sectionOrArticle: Articles XII, XIV & XV: Sin After Justification, Purgatory & Unknown Tongue
citation: Wesleyan Articles of Religion, Art. XII, XIV, XV (1784)
topic: Repentance for Backsliders, Rejection of Purgatory, Vernacular Worship
coreDoctrine: After we have received the Holy Ghost, we may depart from grace given, and fall into sin, and by the grace of God we may arise again and amend our lives; the grant of repentance is not to be denied to such as fall into sin after justification (Art. XII). The Romish doctrine concerning purgatory, pardons, worshiping and adoration of images and relics, and invocation of saints, is a fond thing, vainly invented, and grounded upon no warranty of Scripture (Art. XIV). Public prayer and ministering the sacraments in a tongue not understood by the people is repugnant to the Word of God (Art. XV).
fullExcerpt: Not every sin willingly committed after justification is the sin against the Holy Ghost, and unpardonable. Wherefore, the grant of repentance is not to be denied to such as fall into sin after justification: after we have received the Holy Ghost, we may depart from grace given, and fall into sin, and, by the grace of God, rise again and amend our lives (Art. XII). The Romish doctrine concerning purgatory, pardons, worshiping, and adoration, as well of images as of relics, and also invocation of saints, is a fond thing, vainly invented, and grounded upon no warranty of Scripture, but repugnant to the Word of God (Art. XIV). It is a thing plainly repugnant to the Word of God, and the custom of the primitive Church, to have public prayer in the church, or to minister the Sacraments, in a tongue not understood by the people (Art. XV).

sectionOrArticle: Articles XVI, XVII & XVIII: Of Sacraments, Baptism & The Lord’s Supper
citation: Wesleyan Articles of Religion, Art. XVI–XVIII (1784)
topic: The Two Sacraments, Infant Baptism & Holy Communion
coreDoctrine: Sacraments ordained of Christ are not only badges or tokens of Christian men’s profession, but rather certain signs of grace. There are two Sacraments ordained of Christ our Lord in the Gospel: Baptism, and the Supper of the Lord (Art. XVI). Baptism is a sign of regeneration or the new birth; the baptism of young children is to be retained in the Church (Art. XVII). The Supper of the Lord is a Sacrament of our redemption by Christ’s death; transubstantiation cannot be proved by holy writ, but the body of Christ is given, taken, and eaten in the Supper only after a heavenly and spiritual manner received by faith (Art. XVIII).
fullExcerpt: Sacraments ordained of Christ are not only badges or tokens of Christian men’s profession, but rather they are certain signs of grace, and God’s good will toward us, by which He doth work invisibly in us, and doth not only quicken, but also strengthen and confirm, our faith in Him. There are two Sacraments ordained of Christ our Lord in the Gospel; that is to say, Baptism and the Supper of the Lord (Art. XVI). Baptism is not only a sign of profession and mark of difference whereby Christians are distinguished from others that are not baptized; but it is also a sign of regeneration or the new birth. The baptism of young children is to be retained in the Church (Art. XVII). The Supper of the Lord is not only a sign of the love that Christians ought to have among themselves one to another, but rather is a Sacrament of our redemption by Christ’s death... The body of Christ is given, taken, and eaten in the Supper, only after a heavenly and spiritual manner. And the mean whereby the body of Christ is received and eaten in the Supper is faith (Art. XVIII).

sectionOrArticle: Articles XIX–XXV: Both Kinds, One Oblation, Marriage of Ministers, Civil Rulers
citation: Wesleyan Articles of Religion, Art. XIX–XXV (1784)
topic: Communion in Both Kinds, One Oblation of Christ, Marriage of Ministers, Civil Rulers
coreDoctrine: The Lord’s cup is not to be denied to the lay people (Art. XIX). The offering of Christ, once made, is that perfect redemption, propitiation, and satisfaction for all the sins of the whole world, both original and actual; and there is none other satisfaction for sin but that alone; wherefore the sacrifice of the Mass is a dangerous deceit (Art. XX). The ministers of Christ are not commanded to abstain from marriage (Art. XXI). It is the duty of all Christians to be subject to the supreme authority of the country where they reside (Art. XXIII). Christian men may lend, give alms, and swear lawful oaths (Art. XXIV, XXV).
fullExcerpt: The cup of the Lord is not to be denied to the lay people; for both parts of the Lord’s Supper, by Christ’s ordinance and commandment, ought to be administered to all Christians alike (Art. XIX). The offering of Christ, once made, is that perfect redemption, propitiation, and satisfaction for all the sins of the whole world, both original and actual; and there is none other satisfaction for sin but that alone. Wherefore the sacrifice of the Mass, in the which it is commonly said that the priest doth offer Christ for the quick and the dead, to have remission of pain or guilt, is a blasphemous fable and dangerous deceit (Art. XX). The ministers of Christ are not commanded by God’s law either to vow the estate of single life, or to abstain from marriage; therefore it is lawful for them to marry at their own discretion (Art. XXI). The President, the Congress, the General Assemblies, the Governors, and the Councils of State are the rulers of the United States of America... and we believe it is the duty of all Christians to be subject to the supreme authority of the country where they may reside (Art. XXIII).

topic: Salvation by Grace Through Faith; Justification and New Birth
coreDoctrine: Salvation is entirely by grace through faith in Jesus Christ; this faith is not a mere speculative belief, but a full reliance on the blood of Christ, bringing peace with God, deliverance from the guilt and power of sin, and the inward witness of the Spirit.
fullExcerpt: What faith is it through which we are saved? It is not barely the faith of a heathen, nor the faith of a devil, nor the faith of the Apostles while Christ was yet in the flesh. It is a faith in Christ: Christ, and God through Christ, are the proper objects of it. It is a full reliance on the blood of Christ; a trust in the merits of His life, death, and resurrection; a recumbency upon Him as our atonement and our life, as given for us, and living in us. By this faith we are saved from the guilt of all past sin, and from the power of present sin (Eph. 2:8; Rom. 5:1).

sectionOrArticle: Sermon 40: Christian Perfection & A Plain Account of Christian Perfection
topic: Entire Sanctification and Christian Perfection (Heart Cleansed from Inward Sin)
coreDoctrine: Christian perfection is the loving God with all our heart, mind, soul, and strength, implying that no contrary temper—neither ire, pride, self-will, nor love of the world—remains in the soul, through total cleansing by the Holy Spirit, while acknowledging that bodily infirmities and involuntary mistakes remain.
fullExcerpt: What is Christian perfection? It is loving God with all our heart, mind, soul, and strength. This implies that no wrong temper, none contrary to love, remains in the soul; and that all the thoughts, words, and actions are governed by pure love. Does this imply an exemption from ignorance, mistake, infirmities, or temptations? By no means. Man in this life is not exempt from involuntary mistakes or bodily infirmities; hence even the most perfect continually need the atoning blood of Christ, saying: "Forgive us our trespasses." But by the sanctifying power of the Holy Spirit, the heart may be cleansed from all voluntary sin (1 Thess. 5:23-24, 1 John 1:7-9).

sectionOrArticle: Sermon 43: The Scripture Way of Salvation
topic: The Ordo Salutis: Prevenient, Convincing, Justifying, and Sanctifying Grace
coreDoctrine: Salvation begins with prevenient grace restoring human faculty to respond, progresses to repentance, justification and the new birth through faith, and culminates in entire sanctification wherein we are saved from all sin.
fullExcerpt: Salvation begins with what is usually termed prevenient grace, including the first wish to please God, the first dawn of light concerning His will, and the first slight conviction of having sinned against Him. Salvation is then carried on by convincing grace (repentance). Then follows justification, the forgiveness of sins, and the new birth (initial sanctification). Finally, entire sanctification is that grand promise of God through the Spirit, whereby He circumcises the heart to love the Lord our God with all our heart and with all our soul.

documentTitle: The General Rules of the Methodist Societies
citation: General Rules of the United Societies (1743)
topic: The Three Simple Rules: Do No Harm, Do Good, Attend Upon Ordinances
coreDoctrine: There is only one condition previously required of those who desire admission into these societies: a desire to flee from the wrath to come, and to be saved from their sins. This desire is shown by: (1) Doing no harm, (2) Doing good of every possible sort, and (3) Attending upon all the ordinances of God.
fullExcerpt: There is only one condition previously required of those who desire admission into these societies: "a desire to flee from the wrath to come, and to be saved from their sins." But wherever this is really fixed in the soul it will be shown by its fruits. It is therefore expected of all who continue therein that they should continue to evidence their desire of salvation: First: By doing no harm, by avoiding evil of every kind... Secondly: By doing good; by being in every kind merciful after their power; as they have opportunity, doing good of every possible sort, and, as far as possible, to all men... Thirdly: By attending upon all the ordinances of God; such are: The public worship of God; The ministry of the Word, either read or expounded; The Supper of the Lord; Family and private prayer; Searching the Scriptures; Fasting or abstinence.

documentTitle: Explanatory Notes Upon the New Testament (John Wesley)
topic: Universal Sinfulness Derived from Adam & Mary’s Need of a Savior
coreDoctrine: All human beings naturally descending from Adam have sinned and stand in need of the redemption wrought by Christ alone; Mary’s joyful exclamation "My spirit hath rejoiced in God my Saviour" demonstrates her dependence on God’s saving grace.
fullExcerpt: On Romans 5:12: "As by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned" - Through the disobedience of Adam, all his descendants became guilty and depraved, needing the free gift of righteousness through Jesus Christ. On Luke 1:47: "And my spirit hath rejoiced in God my Saviour" - Mary herself humbly and gladly acknowledges God as her Savior, for she, like all the children of Adam, was redeemed and preserved by the pure grace and mercy of the Almighty through the coming Messiah. On Hebrews 7:25: "He is able to save to the uttermost them that come unto God by him" - He saves from all the guilt, all the power, and all the in-being of sin.
